title: Learning to Theorize the World from Observation
claim: Prediction-centric models memorize entangled composites and fail on novel combinations; learning reusable primitives and composing them generalizes.
layout: 5 panels in 2 rows; training data left, ours top, baseline bottom
description: Panel (a), a tall column on the left, shows four input→output pairs of small colored blocks on black backgrounds, each with a transformation such as left, down, rotate or paint. The right side is split into two rows. The top row is panel (b), Learning to Theorize. It shows colored arrows labeled z_l, z_d, z_r and z_p chaining grayed-box steps, with 'Discover Primitives' and 'Learn to Compose' arrows pointing to a list of four primitives. Below it, panel (c), Prediction-centric Approach, shows single arrows with entangled labels such as z_ld and z_rp, and a list of entangled programs. Panel (d), top right, composes learned primitives into a novel theory that equals the target, marked with a green check. Panel (e), bottom right, shows the entangled paths giving an output that does not equal the target, marked with a red not-equal sign.
caption: Learning to Theorize (L2T) Framework. (a) Training data consists of observation pairs $(x,y)$ generated by unobserved true programs. (b) Under L2T, the model learns to discover reusable primitives (Rotate, Left, Down, and Paint) and to compose them into executable theories. (c) Without L2T, the model instead memorizes entangled composite primitives (e.g., Left-Down) as indecomposed single units. (d) Once the model has learned to theorize, novel phenomena (e.g., Down-Paint-Rotate) can be explained by recombining learned primitives. (e) In contrast, memorized entangled representations fail to generalize to unseen programs.
abstract: What does it mean to understand the world? Contemporary world models often operationalize understanding as accurate future prediction in latent or observation space. Developmental cognitive science, however, suggests a different view: human understanding emerges through the construction of internal theories of how the world works, even before mature language is acquired. Inspired by this theory-building view of cognition, we introduce Learning-to-Theorize, a learning paradigm for inferring explicit explanatory theories of the world from raw, non-textual observations. We instantiate this paradigm with the Neural Theorizer (NEO), a World Theory Model, that induces latent programs as a learned Language of Thought and executes them through a shared transition model. In NEO, a theory is represented as an executable, compositional program whose learned primitives can be systematically recombined to explain novel phenomena. Experiments show that this formulation enables explanation-driven generalization, allowing observations to be understood in terms of the programs that generate them.
